summary: Presents the Topology-Transparent Zone for an OSPF area, a group of routers and links whose internal topology is hidden from routers outside. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A black box inside the map: outsiders see just the box, not what is inside.

subtitle: Hide the internal structure of a group of routers from the rest of the network.

tldr.problem: OSPF networks often grow large and need reorganization, but moving routers between areas causes service interruptions and requires reconfiguring many routers.
tldr.mechanism: A Topology-Transparent Zone (TTZ) is a group of routers whose internal topology is hidden from routers outside the zone. External routers see only the zone's edge routers connected together, not the internal details.
tldr.outcome: Networks can be reorganized without disrupting service. Internal topology changes do not cause routing instability outside the zone.

facts.label: Edge Router Type
facts.value: Some links inside, some outside zone

today: RFC 8099 specifies an Experimental protocol for OSPF. It has not been obsoleted and remains a proposed technique for network reorganization. Implementations have validated the concept, though adoption in production networks has been limited.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.content:
OSPF networks expand over time as business grows and traffic increases. A hierarchical network organized into areas is standard practice for scalability. However, reorganizing a network from one area into multiple areas or consolidating areas is challenging and disruptive.

When reorganizing, each interface with an area change must transition down and up with the new area, causing service interruptions. Additionally, reconfiguring the network topology requires careful design to maintain backbone continuity and ensure all areas remain reachable.

RFC 8099 presents the Topology-Transparent Zone (TTZ) to resolve these issues. A TTZ allows a group of routers and links to be managed transparently. External routers do not see the internal topology; only the zone's edge routers and their connections outside the zone are advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: A TTZ is like putting some routers in a black box. Routers outside the box cannot see what's inside, only what the box's doors connect to. This makes it easier to reorganize the network without breaking things.

sections.title: TTZ Concepts and Topology
sections.content:
A TTZ comprises routers and links organized within a single OSPF area. Each TTZ has a unique 32-bit identifier. Two types of routers exist in a TTZ: TTZ-internal routers, which have all their links within the zone, and TTZ edge routers, which have some links inside and some outside the zone.

From the perspective of a router outside the TTZ, the zone appears as its edge routers fully meshed together. A TTZ hides the internal topology completely. External routers do not learn about TTZ-internal routers or the links between them. When a link fails inside the zone or a TTZ-internal router goes down, this information is not advertised outside.

TTZ-external routers see the edge routers as normal routers with connections to external routers and to other edge routers in the TTZ. The full mesh of virtual connections between edge routers is maintained automatically as TTZ information is exchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of edge routers as doors and internal routers as desks inside an office. External visitors only see which doors are connected to the outside and to each other, not where the desks are inside.

sections.title: Protocol Extensions for TTZ
sections.content:
OSPF is extended to support TTZ using opaque LSAs (Link-State Advertisements) of type 10 and type 9. Four types of TTZ LSAs are defined:

  • TTZ Router LSA: Originated by TTZ edge routers. Contains TTZ ID and router link information about both internal and external links.
  • TTZ Indication LSA: Originated by TTZ-internal routers. Indicates that the originator is internal to the zone.
  • TTZ Control LSA: Carries control information for operations such as migration and rollback, using TTZ Options TLVs.
  • TTZ Discovery LSA: Link-scoped LSA used for discovering TTZ neighbors over a single link.

Three TLV types are defined: TTZ ID TLV (contains the zone identifier and flags), TTZ Router TLV (carries link state information), and TTZ Options TLV (controls migration and rollback operations).
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF is taught new message types to communicate TTZ information. Some messages say 'I am a door to the TTZ', some say 'I am inside the TTZ', and some say 'let's reorganize now'.

sections.title: Migration, Operation, and Configuration
sections.content:
Configuring a TTZ involves marking links or routers with the same TTZ ID. The RFC defines two configuration methods: marking each TTZ link individually, or marking routers and their zone-connecting links. A TTZ edge router can connect multiple zones.

Migration to TTZ proceeds in three stages. First, operators configure the TTZ on all routers. Second, operators trigger one router to advertise TTZ topology information, which propagates to all zone routers. Third, operators trigger migration on one router, which propagates to all routers in the zone.

When migrating to TTZ, edge routers perform a two-step process to advertise their router LSA. They first add virtual point-to-point links to other edge routers and stub links for advertised loopback addresses. After waiting for updates from other edge routers to propagate, they remove the actual zone links. This prevents routing disruptions during the transition.

Rollback from TTZ is performed in reverse order. Operators can add routers to an existing TTZ by configuring the TTZ ID on the new router and its connecting link.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a TTZ is like gradually closing a door. First you tell everyone the door exists, then you step through it, then you slowly move all your stuff through. You can also add more rooms to the group later.

sections.title: Implementation and Security
sections.content:
A prototype implementation demonstrated that TTZ works as specified. Internal topology information is successfully contained within the zone and is not advertised to external routers. Smooth migration is possible without routing disruptions. The implementation reuses existing OSPF code with additional logic for TTZ operations.

From a security perspective, TTZ provides a beneficial masking of internal topology. External routers do not learn about the zone's internal structure. However, a malicious node could inject TTZ LSAs with migration or rollback operations, potentially causing routing isolation. Operators should reuse OSPF authentication mechanisms and the security extensions in RFC 7474 to mitigate such risks.
sections.plainLanguage: Programmers have tested the TTZ system and it works. One security concern is that a bad actor could send fake 'reorganize' messages, but OSPF already has ways to prevent this.
